On March 15, 2022, I received an email that changed the course of my life. It was a likely letter from Cornell University, letting me know that I would be offered admission to the Class of 2026. As a first-generation college student, neither of my parents had the opportunity to attend university. That email opened a door that no one in my immediate family had ever walked through. Four years later, I'm excited to share that I graduated Summa Cum Laude from Cornell University with a B.A. in Computer Science and Mathematics, and was elected to the Phi Beta Kappa honor society. I was also honored to receive the Jonathan E. Marx Memorial Senior Prize at graduation, awarded in recognition of exceptional scholarship, leadership, and service to the Cornell community. None of this would have been possible without my family. To my parents, who sacrificed so much and believed in a dream they never had the chance to pursue themselves: this degree is as much yours as it is mine. I'm also deeply grateful to the professors and mentors who challenged me and believed in me, the friends who made Cornell feel like home, and the students I had the privilege of teaching. Serving as a TA was one of the most rewarding parts of my undergraduate experience. I set out to help students grow, and I ended up learning just as much from them. I'm also thankful for the opportunity to lead the development of Cornell's Course Management System (CMS). Building software that thousands of students and instructors rely on every semester was an amazing experience, and I'm grateful to the faculty and students who trusted me with that responsibility. Cornell challenged me in ways I never expected. The coursework, the opportunities, and the people around me constantly pushed me to think more deeply, work harder, and hold myself to a very high standard. Walking across the graduation stage was emotional, not just because it marked the end of four years, but because I realized how far I've come since opening that email in March 2022. This fall, I'm excited to begin the next chapter as an M.S. student in Computer Science at Carnegie Mellon University, where I will further study ML and CS, conduct research, and build on everything Cornell taught me. Thank you, Cornell, for believing in me and giving me opportunities that changed my life. I'll always be grateful. Cornell University , Carnegie Mellon University , Carnegie Mellon University School of Computer Science

Quantum hardware remains too noisy for consistent results, and Q-CTRL is building the software layer to fix that. I recently discussed the company's approach with Alex Shih, its vice president of product. Shih walked me through how Q-CTRL's error-reduction software works with hardware vendors and with enterprises testing quantum applications on real machines. He described a deployment with Elevate Quantum in Colorado that moved from concept to a working system in five months. He added that ColibriTD and Qunova Computing are part of a growing group of partners building their own applications on top of Q-CTRL's pipeline. Here are some key takeaways from our talk: --He expects quantum advantage in specific workflows within two to three years, with optimization leading. In a Mazda case study he shared, quantum methods needed five times less training data to reach the same vehicle frame design. --He pointed to Riken, a Japanese lab home to the Fugaku supercomputer and an IBM quantum system, where Q-CTRL's software supports the lab's exploration of hybrid quantum-classical computing. --He shared that Q-CTRL measures success by how accessible its tools are to companies worldwide, not by papers published. Read the full article: https://lnkd.in/gKHr_aXS

Ten years ago, Amazon's Automated Reasoning Group set out to use mathematical logic to prove AWS systems work correctly. Today, their production services process billions of queries daily, powering tools millions of customers rely on, from IAM Access Analyzer to Amazon Inspector to Bedrock Guardrails. One project stands out: they proved correct and seamlessly replaced the AWS authorization engine, which handles one billion API calls per second, and verified it against quadrillions of production authorizations. Now the same formal-verification techniques that secured cloud infrastructure are being applied to AI, setting boundaries for autonomous agents and validating AI-generated content with up to 99% verification accuracy.

This summer I've had the opportunity to work as an undergraduate researcher in the Kaufman Lab at UW–Madison, under Prof. Alfonso Morales , contributing to two full stack projects focused on food access and equity, Thankfully I'll be continuing under this lab for the upcoming academic year. It's been a great deep dive into concurrency, complexity analysis, and building simulation infrastructure that can actually scale. I had the chance to present a research poster, "Engineering FEAST: Building A Platform for Food Access Simulation," at the LASER symposium which was a great opportunity to share this work with the wider research community.

As a student on the quarter system, my summer CPT overlaps with Snowflake’s required Fall internship start window, and unfortunately there was no way to make the transition work. Kara (YC S26) engineers ultra-high-purity diamond wafers and components for the next generation of hardware. Modern hardware is getting more powerful, smaller, and hotter. AI accelerators in data centers throttle and deliver less compute when heat builds up. High-power RF and lasers lose performance. Aircraft and spacecraft carry heavy cooling systems. Heat is becoming a hard limit on performance. Kara is engineering the hardest material to push that limit. They grow ultra-high-purity diamond wafers and components that transfer heat 5x faster than copper while weighing 60% less. They're already shipping diamond wafers under pilot agreements and purchase orders for data centers, aerospace, and quantum systems. The three founders are best friends from UC Berkeley. Aarin Jhaveri is a fifth-generation diamantaire who has worked across the supply chain and sold millions worth of diamonds. Anuveer Chadha is a chemical engineer who built diamond quantum sensing and advanced materials systems at Berkeley National Lab with the Department of Defense and Department of Energy. Arjun Lakhanpal brings AI/ML experience from Amazon and thermal management research from Berkeley’s Space Sciences Lab. Diamond is their unfair advantage: they know how to grow, control, and engineer it far beyond jewelry. Silicon transformed computing when we learned to manufacture it with extreme purity and control. Kara is doing the same with diamond. Today, their ultra-high-purity diamond pulls heat away from silicon chips. Tomorrow, Kara’s control over purity and defects unlocks diamond as the ultimate semiconductor. Kara is building the diamond computing era. If you’re building hardware where heat, power density or weight is becoming the limit, reach out at founders@karalabs.ai Congrats on the launch, Aarin, Anuveer, and Arjun! 🚀 https://lnkd.in/g-uigUBs
